title: The Sorrows of Young Werther
author: Johann Wolfgang von Goethe
length: Two books of letters and a closing account · 84 reading units
openingText: I have gathered with care everything I could learn about the story of poor Werther, and I set it before you here, certain that you will thank me for it. You cannot withhold your admiration and love from his spirit and character, nor your tears from his fate.
about:
Werther moves to the countryside, takes pleasure in nature, and meets Charlotte, who cares for her younger siblings and is engaged to Albert. He falls in love with her and writes to his friend Wilhelm about their meetings, his happiness, and his growing despair.

The novel contains two books of dated letters and a closing account in which an editor assembles testimony and surviving papers. Werther's attempt to settle into diplomatic employment, his encounters with social rank, and his return to Charlotte all shape the story. The landscape that first comforts him gradually becomes an image of threatening forces.

Goethe's novel first appeared in 1774 and was revised in 1787. This reading text includes the expanded story, including the farm servant's unhappy attachment. Watch the differences between what Werther feels, what he claims about other people, and what the editor later reports. The story ends with Werther's suicide; his interpretation of his situation is itself something the novel asks us to examine.

angleCards.title: Nature changes its meaning
angleCards.text: The spring, the trees, and everyday life initially comfort Werther. Later he sees destruction in nature. Follow the concrete images and distinguish changes in the landscape from changes in the observer.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to follow the descriptions of nature and their relationship to Werther's changing feelings.

angleCards.title: Love, friendship, and boundaries
angleCards.text: Charlotte cares for Werther but is engaged and later married to Albert. Werther interprets her looks and words through his own longing. Where does he understand her, and where do his wishes shape his beliefs?
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to examine Werther's relationships with Charlotte and Albert, distinguishing feelings, assumptions, and actions.

angleCards.title: A person within a hierarchy
angleCards.text: Werther encounters rules of class and rank in employment and society. He reacts strongly to humiliation, yet also describes others through their social positions. Follow both sides of his outlook.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to examine how class and working life shape Werther's choices and his understanding of other people.

angleCards.title: Letters and testimony
angleCards.text: We read Werther's letters but not Wilhelm's replies. At the end, the editor compares several accounts and acknowledges the difficulty of knowing people's motives. Notice what this change does to the story.
angleCards.angleObjective: I want to compare Werther's own account with the editor's presentation of his last days.

cast.name: Werther
cast.description: A young man who draws, reads, and experiences his surroundings intensely. He writes to Wilhelm about nature, employment, other people's lives, and his love for Charlotte. His letters reveal both his feelings and the limits of his understanding of others.

cast.name: Charlotte
cast.description: A young woman who cares for her younger siblings after their mother's death. She is engaged and later married to Albert. Her friendship with Werther becomes increasingly difficult to reconcile with the boundaries she tries to establish.

cast.name: Albert
cast.description: Werther initially describes him respectfully and debates suicide with him. Their relationship later becomes strained. The editor also reports Albert's friends' explanation of his behavior.

cast.name: Wilhelm
cast.role: The friend who receives the letters
cast.description: We know his advice through Werther's replies. He urges Werther to act and consider other possibilities, but his own letters are not included.

cast.name: The editor
cast.description: An unnamed editor introduces the book and later takes over the narrative. He gathers letters and testimony, distinguishes different explanations, and relates Werther's last days.

cast.name: Homer and Ossian
cast.description: Homer accompanies Werther in happier months. Later he prefers Ossian's stories of loss and dead heroes. His reading to Charlotte becomes an important scene in the closing account.

whyItMatters.title: Feelings also interpret
whyItMatters.body: The letters bring us close to Werther's joy and pain. The novel also shows how feelings direct what he sees and believes about others. Sympathy and critical reading can work together.

whyItMatters.title: Other lives reflect the protagonist
whyItMatters.body: The children, the farm servant, and the former clerk do more than supply background. Werther uses their lives to understand his own; readers can examine both the similarities and what his comparisons overlook.

whyItMatters.title: The narrative changes perspective
whyItMatters.body: The editor makes room for other voices and shows how difficult it is to establish motives. The closing account tests explanations we have received through the letters.
